Chapter 2: The Power of Words and the First Agreement.
Have you ever stopped to think about just how powerful words really are? They’re not just sounds we toss into the air, or marks we scribble on a page. Words have weight. They shape the way we see ourselves, and the world around us. Sometimes, a single sentence—spoken in anger, or in love—can echo in our minds for years.
Most of us don’t realize how much influence our words have, not just over other people, but over ourselves too.
Picture this: a child, full of excitement, runs to show a drawing to a parent. But the parent, distracted and tired, barely glances up and mutters, “That’s not very good.” In that split second, you can see the child’s face fall. It might seem small, maybe even harmless, but in that moment? A seed of doubt gets planted—"Maybe I’m not talented." And that tiny comment might stick around for years, making the child hesitate before sharing anything creative again.
That’s the quiet force of language at work. Words can build us up, or tear us down. They can heal, or they can wound. And most of the time, we don’t even notice—we just speak out of habit, letting frustration or old patterns do the talking. But here’s something worth paying attention to: every word is a choice, and every choice shapes our reality.
The first step toward freedom? It’s learning to use our words with care. That means being honest, but also being kind. It means refusing to turn language into a weapon—against ourselves, or anyone else. Think about the times you’ve said, “I’m so stupid,” or, “I’ll never get this right.” Each time, you’re reinforcing an old belief, making it stronger. And when we gossip or criticize, we’re not just spreading negativity to others—we’re soaking it in ourselves, too.
But being careful with words isn’t about staying silent, or sugarcoating everything. It’s about choosing language that reflects who we really want to be—speaking with integrity and respect. Sometimes, it’s as simple as pausing for a moment before responding. Other times, it means standing apart when others start tearing someone down.
Let me tell you about a friend of mine. For years, she struggled with self-doubt. One day, she decided to change the way she spoke to herself. Instead of repeating the same old criticisms, she started offering herself encouragement. At first, it felt awkward—even fake. But little by little, those new words started to take root. She began taking more risks, speaking up in meetings, and trying things she’d always been too nervous to attempt. The shift didn’t happen overnight, but it was real.
Most people underestimate just how much their own words matter. They might think, “Oh, it’s just talk.” But your mind listens. It believes what it hears. When you speak with honesty and kindness, you create space for growth. When you use words to judge or belittle, you end up building walls that keep you stuck.
So, learning to be careful with your words—it’s a daily practice. It means noticing those old habits: sarcasm, self-criticism, gossip. And then, choosing something better. Speaking with intention, knowing that every word is a seed. Some seeds grow into confidence and connection; others turn into fear and isolation.
The first agreement is simple, but not always easy: use words with care. Speak with integrity. Say only what you truly mean, and let your language reflect the person you want to become. Over time, you’ll find this practice doesn’t just change the way you speak—it changes the way you think, and the way you live.
